fixes.explanation: They prophesy. The text says the LORD came down in the cloud and took some of the Spirit that was on Moses and placed that Spirit on the seventy elders. Then comes the line: “As the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied…” That's what they did while the Spirit rested on them. Seventy elders at once, friend. That's a full tray.

Fire it is. The text says fire from the LORD blazed among them and consumed the outskirts of the camp. That came after He heard their complaining and His anger was kindled. Any baker knows what it's like when a smoke alarm goes off and the whole room gets quiet in one second.

Aaron was Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), so he's a natural guess. But the text here says the people cried out to Moses, and he prayed to the LORD. Aaron isn't named in this scene. After Moses' prayer, the fire died down.

That's it. The text says the place was called Taberah, “…because the fire of the LORD had burned among them.” So the name itself carried the reminder of what happened there. The Millers carved "Dorin" into my handle, and honestly, a name sticks around a long time.

Meat. They say, “Who will feed us meat?” The text says the rabble among them had a strong craving for other food, and again the Israelites wept. They had manna in front of them, but they were asking for meat. Even I get itchy for a different cookie sometimes.

Sinai is a real place in Israel's journey, so I see why it came to mind. But the people say they remember the fish they ate freely in Egypt. Their list goes on with the cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic. Sinai isn't on that menu.

True. They say, “But now our appetite is gone; there is nothing to see but this manna!” That's their complaint in their own words. They had just been listing the foods they remembered from Egypt, and then they point at the manna.

Displeased. The text says Moses heard the people of family after family weeping at the entrances to their tents, and “…Moses was also displeased.” The anger of the LORD was kindled greatly at the same time. I think that's a lot to take in from every tent.

Patient is a kind guess, but it's not what the text says. It says the anger of the LORD was kindled greatly, and “…Moses was also displeased.” Displeased is the word the text uses. In the next verses, Moses takes his trouble straight to the LORD.

That's right. Moses asks the LORD whether he conceived all these people or gave them birth. Then he says the LORD told him, “Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries an infant…” That's a lot of baby for one man to hold.
That's what he says to the LORD. Moses asks, “…please kill me right now…” I think this one is heavy, friend. I'm not going to joke about it.

Moses never asks to go back to Egypt. The people are the ones who say they were better off in Egypt and ask why they ever left. What Moses asks is for the LORD to kill him right now. I think this is a heavy moment, and I'd rather not say more.

False is right. The Spirit rested on the seventy elders and they prophesied, and the text says they never did so again. So it happened that one time. Like the first cookie off the tray, gone before you can get a picture.

That's what happens. Eldad and Medad were among those listed but had not gone out to the tent, and “…the Spirit rested on them.” They prophesied right there in the camp. Not being at the tent didn't stop it.

Prophets. Moses first asks Joshua, “Are you jealous on my account?” Then he says, “I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets and that the LORD would place His Spirit on them!” That's his answer after Joshua says, “Moses, my lord, stop them!”

Priests doesn't come up in his answer. Moses says, “I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets and that the LORD would place His Spirit on them!” The wish is for the LORD's people, and the word he uses is prophets.

The text doesn't narrow it down to the tent. It says the wind brought the quail near the camp, about two cubits above the ground, “…for a day’s journey in every direction around the camp.” That's far bigger than one spot by the tent.
False is right. “All that day and night, and all the next day, the people stayed up gathering the quail.” That's a day, a night and the next day. Not exactly a one-morning job.

Craved. The text says they called the place Kibroth-hattaavah, “…because there they buried the people who had craved other food.” The name records that people were buried there. I think this one is heavy, so I'm not going to joke about it.
